strengths: Novel and well-motivated framing: the paper identifies an underexplored economic angle of tokenization — that pay-per-token pricing creates an informational asymmetry (moral hazard) enabling providers to overcharge users by misreporting tokenizations — and situates it properly in the principal-agent and mechanism design literature.

Clean and correct-looking theoretical contribution: Theorem 6 gives an exact characterization of additive incentive-compatible pricing mechanisms (pricing must be linear in character counts), which is elegant and directly yields the pay-per-character proposal; Proposition 5 is a useful intermediate step and the proofs in Appendix B appear sound.

The NP-hardness result (Theorem 3) for finding the longest plausible tokenization under top-p sampling, with extensions to top-k and probability-threshold plausibility (Appendix B.1), is a nice complement to the empirical work and is backed by a correct Hamiltonian-path reduction.

Experiments across five open-weight LLMs (Llama, Gemma, Ministral) using LMSYS prompts, with confidence intervals from repeated runs, demonstrate that the proposed heuristic can realistically overcharge users by up to ~13% while remaining plausible — a non-trivial empirical demonstration that computational hardness does not protect users.

Honest and thorough limitations discussion (additive mechanisms only, stylized threat model, non-representative prompts, need for external regulation, dual-use concerns of the heuristic), plus good attention to licenses and reproducibility details (hardware, seeds, dataset filtering, per-model sources).
weaknesses: The practical significance of the threat model is questionable: real API providers are large, reputation-constrained firms subject to audit and regulation, and the paper provides no evidence of actual misreporting in practice. The core 'vulnerability' may be more of a theoretical observation than a pressing real-world problem, which limits impact.

The main characterization theorem is conceptually straightforward: Proposition 5 (IC implies price depends only on the string) combined with additivity almost immediately forces per-character pricing. The result is clean but not deep, and the assumption of additive mechanisms excludes other natural pricing families (the paper only discusses these as future work).

The NP-hardness construction uses artificial, adversarially designed next-token distributions rather than distributions arising from real LLMs; while standard for hardness results, this limits its bearing on whether real providers face computational barriers.

Experimental scope is narrow: only 400 filtered English prompts from a single source (LMSYS), outputs of fixed length (200-300 tokens), and the plausibility check assumes the user can access or verify next-token probabilities — a strong transparency assumption that proprietary providers are unlikely to satisfy, making the 'without raising suspicion' setting partly hypothetical.

The trivial attack (reporting every character as a token, ~3x overcharge in Table 1) is predictable from the model definition and adds little; the interesting heuristic results are confined to relatively modest gains (0.3-13%) that depend on high temperatures (>1.0) and lenient top-p values, and are unimodal in the iteration count in ways that are only empirically characterized.

The pay-per-character proposal has been implicitly used elsewhere (per-character/character-based billing predates token pricing), so the policy contribution is more a formalization than a new mechanism; the downstream-efficiency argument (incentive to shorten outputs) is asserted but not experimentally validated.

strengths: The paper is well written and clearly organized, framing tokenization misreporting in LLM-as-a-service as a principal-agent (moral hazard) problem, which is a fresh angle connecting tokenization to mechanism design.

The theoretical package is coherent: Theorem 6 gives a clean characterization that any additive incentive-compatible mechanism must price linearly in per-character counts, immediately yielding the pay-per-character mechanism; the NP-hardness reduction (Theorem 3) and its extensions to top-k and probability-threshold plausibility (Appendix B) are carefully executed.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably thorough: five open-weight LLMs across three families, multiple temperature and top-p settings, repeated runs with confidence intervals, exhaustive tokenization enumeration for Figure 1, and qualitative examples of modified tokenizations in Appendix C.2.

The limitations and broader-impact discussion is honest and substantive, explicitly acknowledging the stylized threat model, alternative misreporting avenues not covered, the unrepresentativeness of LMSYS prompts, and the dual-use nature of Algorithm 1.
weaknesses: The core observation has limited depth: that a provider with unobservable token counts could overcharge under pay-per-token pricing is fairly intuitive, and a provider unconstrained by 'plausibility' can simply lie about token counts arbitrarily. The paper's most interesting setting—a provider that discloses next-token distributions—does not correspond to how commercial providers actually operate, weakening the practical relevance of the central threat model.

The NP-hardness result, while correct, is established on a pathological construction (a vocabulary of 'a'-only tokens with hand-designed next-token distributions encoding a Hamiltonian path instance). It does not establish hardness for realistic LLM vocabularies or distributions, so the claim that 'misreporting optimally without raising suspicion is hard' has limited bite for the systems the paper studies empirically.

The practical impact of the demonstrated attack is modest: the maximum overcharge is ~13%, achieved only under favorable conditions (p=0.99, temperature 1.3, Llama-3.2-1B), with most settings yielding a few percent or less, and Algorithm 1 finds a longer plausible tokenization for only a minority of outputs (often <20% and decreasing quickly in m).

The proposed remedy, pay-per-character pricing, is an obvious solution once the problem is stated, and its characterization (Theorem 6) follows from short, straightforward arguments; the paper's main theorems feel more like careful formalization than substantial technical contribution.

Reproducibility is weakened by the apparent absence of released code; the experimental setup is described but no artifact is referenced, and the prompt filtering (first 400 English prompts of length 20-100 characters) is a narrow sample, as the authors themselves concede.

Significance is specialized: the contribution speaks to a niche intersection of tokenization and pricing economics, and the paper does not demonstrate that the vulnerability matters for the proprietary APIs that dominate practice (which are neither transparent nor verifiable by users).

strengths: Novel and interesting framing: the paper identifies a previously unexplored economic vulnerability of pay-per-token pricing for LLM-as-a-service, connecting tokenization non-uniqueness to a principal-agent (moral hazard) problem. This is a fresh angle at the intersection of tokenization research and mechanism design.

The theoretical contributions are sound and complete: Proposition 5 and Theorem 6 give a clean, correct characterization of additive incentive-compatible pricing mechanisms (the proof is short but rigorous), and Theorem 3's NP-hardness result for finding the longest plausible tokenization under top-p sampling is a genuine piece of work, with a well-constructed Hamiltonian path reduction and careful extensions to top-k and probability-threshold plausibility in Appendix B.

The empirical evaluation is well designed and transparent: five LLMs across three families, real user prompts from LMSYS Chatbot Arena, repeated runs with confidence intervals, ablations over temperature, p, and number of iterations, plus qualitative examples (Appendix C.2) that make the attack concrete.

Presentation is clear and well organized, and the limitations section is honest and substantive, discussing model assumptions (additive pricing, negligible plausibility-check cost), alternative attack surfaces, the unrepresentativeness of LMSYS prompts, and the dual-use nature of Algorithm 1. Licensing and dataset details are documented.

The paper is largely reproducible: all models are publicly available, the dataset is public, the algorithm is fully specified with complexity analysis, and experimental details (hardware, seeds, filtering criteria, statistical procedure) are provided.
weaknesses: Limited depth of the technical contributions relative to the framing. The core observation (a provider can report each character as a separate token and overcharge ~3x) is straightforward once stated, and the main positive result (pay-per-character pricing is the unique equal-price incentive-compatible mechanism) is nearly immediate from additivity plus the observation that users derive value from the string, not the tokenization. The proofs of Proposition 5 and Theorem 6 span a few lines each.

The threat model is somewhat narrow and arguably understated: a dishonest provider could also misreport the output string, the next-token distributions, or usage counts more broadly. Restricting to string-preserving tokenization misreports is reasonable for a plausibility analysis, but it weakens the practical significance of the incentive-compatibility claim, since a truly malicious provider need not respect it.

Practical significance is uncertain. Real providers face reputational, contractual, and regulatory constraints, and the demonstrated gains from the plausibility-constrained attack are modest (up to ~13% of tokens at p=0.99 and high temperature, dropping to a fraction of a percent at p=0.9). The paper's own limitations section acknowledges that adoption of pay-per-character would likely require external regulation, which is outside the scope of what the paper can establish.

The evaluation is restricted to small open-weight instruct models (1B-8B) and 400 English prompts of length 20-100 characters from a single source whose representativeness the authors themselves question; no proprietary API models are studied, where the mechanism would matter most in practice.

The hardness result, while correct, concerns worst-case constructions (artificial vocabularies and adversarially designed next-token distributions); the paper does not establish that the hardest instances resemble realistic LLM settings, so the computational barrier's practical bite is unclear.

The plausibility criterion under top-p (and its threshold variant) is one reasonable formalization among several; results could be sensitive to this modeling choice, and alternatives are only sketched in appendices.
No code release is explicitly mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the empirical pipeline despite the thorough description.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: the paper is, to my knowledge, the first to formally study incentive-compatibility of token-level pricing in LLM-as-a-service, framing tokenization misreporting as a principal-agent/moral hazard problem. The core observation (tokenization of a string is not unique, and the provider controls the report) is simple, elegant, and consequential.

Solid and clean theory: Theorem 3 (NP-hardness of finding the longest plausible tokenization under top-p sampling, with extensions to top-k and probability-threshold plausibility in Appendices B.1.1–B.1.2) is a correct and well-constructed reduction from Hamiltonian path. Theorem 6 gives a crisp characterization: additive incentive-compatible pricing must be linear in character counts, which directly implies pay-per-token is provably not incentive-compatible (Corollary 7).

The attack (Algorithm 2) is a credible proof-of-concept, and the paper is unusually careful about the economics: it accounts for the GPU cost of verifying plausibility (Figure 11, Table 1) and derives the condition (Eq. 4) under which misreporting is profitable, rather than merely showing longer tokenizations exist.

Experiments are thoughtfully designed: multiple model families (Llama, Gemma, Ministral), real prompts from LMSYS-Chat-1M, repeated runs with 90% confidence intervals, sensitivity analyses over p, temperature, m, provider margin, and language (Appendix C.4), plus direct GPU energy measurements.

Excellent reproducibility and research ethics: code is available, hardware/dataset/model details and licenses are documented, limitations are discussed candidly (non-representativeness of LMSYS prompts, single user–provider micro-level focus, verbosity remains exploitable under pay-per-character), and dual-use concerns are addressed with an appropriate adversarial-ML analogy.

The pay-per-character prescription includes a practical transition rule (rc = ro · tpc) preserving average provider margin, and the analysis of margin distribution across languages (Appendix C.4) adds a nice fairness dimension (minority-language users may benefit).
weaknesses: The central 'vulnerability' result depends on a transparency assumption that is currently hypothetical: the attack requires the provider to disclose next-token distributions and the user to be able to verify plausibility. Real providers do not release next-token distributions, and the paper acknowledges that verifiability (via TEEs/ZKPs) is left as future work. Thus the demonstrated overcharging scenario (up to 11.2% for p=0.99, but only 1.8% at p=0.95 and 0.28% at p=0.90) applies to a setting that does not exist in practice today, weakening the practical urgency of the claim.

The hardness result of Theorem 3 is established for adversarially constructed vocabularies and next-token distributions; it does not by itself establish hardness for the next-token distributions of realistic LLMs, so the gap between 'provably hard in general' and 'hard for real models' remains open.

Experiments use only small open-weight models (1B–8B). Proprietary frontier models, which dominate actual pay-per-token commerce, are not evaluated, and their tokenizers/sampling pipelines could behave differently (the paper notes this but does not mitigate it).

The characterization in Theorem 6, while clean, follows almost immediately from Proposition 5 plus additivity; the theoretical depth is moderate, and the pay-per-character remedy is arguably a fairly foreseeable conclusion once the framing is set.

The magnitude of demonstrated overcharging under realistic sampling settings (p=0.95, p=0.90) is modest, and the profitable regime requires temperatures >1.0 (creative writing), so the practical financial risk for typical workloads appears limited.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely novel problem: the economic incentives that tokenization ambiguity creates for LLM providers under pay-per-token pricing. To my knowledge this is the first formal treatment of incentive-compatible token pricing mechanisms.

The modeling is clean. The principal-agent formulation (Section 2) is well-posed, and Proposition 5 / Theorem 6 give a complete, simple characterization: additive incentive-compatible mechanisms must price tokens linearly in character counts. The proofs (Appendix B) are correct and self-contained.

The NP-hardness result (Theorem 3) is technically sound, with a valid reduction from Hamiltonian path, and the authors thoughtfully extend it to top-k sampling and probability-threshold plausibility criteria (Appendices B.1.1, B.1.2).

Experiments cover multiple model families (Llama, Gemma, Ministral) and include real GPU energy measurements supporting the cost model, and the code availability and license documentation in Appendix A support reproducibility.

The limitations section (Section 5) is unusually candid: it acknowledges that providers can misreport next-token distributions or release a different tokenizer, that pay-per-character does not prevent verbosity inflation, and that the LMSYS prompt distribution may not be representative.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim that providers can 'significantly overcharge users without raising suspicion' is overstated. The reported gains are 11.2% only at p=0.99 and only 1.8% at p=0.95 and 0.28% at p=0.90 (Figure 2), and only for temperature >1.0. Temperature 1.3 is far above what production APIs typically use, and the effects shrink substantially at more realistic settings (Figures 5-7). The headline framing does not match the measured magnitudes.

The threat model does a lot of unsupported work. In the transparency setting, the user must trust that the provider truthfully reports next-token distributions and top-p sets; a provider willing to misreport tokenizations could also misreport these. The authors acknowledge this only in passing in Section 5, yet the entire distinction between the 'hard' optimal-misreporting regime (Theorem 3) and the practical threat is premised on the user's ability to verify plausibility, which no current mechanism provides.

The gap between theory and practice is large. Theorem 3's NP-hardness is established for an artificial construction (alphabet {a}, single-token outputs, adversarially designed next-token distributions), so it says little about realistic BPE vocabularies and distributions. Conversely, Algorithm 2 is so simple that the hardness barrier feels like a distraction rather than a barrier, which undercuts contribution 2.

Theorem 6 is essentially a two-line consequence of Proposition 5 plus additivity, and Proposition 5 itself is immediate. The characterization is neat but its technical depth is modest for a main-track paper.

Internal inconsistencies in the appendix raise reproducibility concerns: Appendix A states experiments run on 2x Nvidia A100 GPUs and that 'a single Nvidia A100 is used' in each experiment, but Figure 11 and Table 1 are captioned as measured on a 'single Nvidia H100'; Appendix A also lists the model 'Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct' (a typo for the 1B model).

The energy-cost assumption c_gen ∝ len(t) is linearized from aggregate measurements, and the claim that verification cost cv is length-independent (used to derive Eq. 4) is only supported empirically on a small model set with one GPU type; the financial-viability conclusions in Figure 3 hinge on this constant.

The prescription for transitioning to pay-per-character (rc = ro·tpc) is a heuristic average with no welfare or mechanism-design analysis; the paper does not compare against any alternative mitigation (e.g., audit mechanisms, TEEs) even descriptively, so the policy recommendation rests on thin ground.

The proposed remedy is regulatorily unrealistic within the paper's own model: Section 5 concedes the provider designs the contract and the user has limited leverage, so the practical impact of the incentive-compatibility result is questionable as presented.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely novel and underexplored problem: the economic incentives that non-unique tokenization creates under pay-per-token pricing in LLM-as-a-service, framing it cleanly as a principal-agent (moral hazard) problem.

The theoretical contributions are clean and correct-looking: the NP-hardness reduction from Hamiltonian path for finding the longest plausible tokenization (Theorem 3) is well-constructed, with sensible extensions to top-k sampling and probability-threshold plausibility (Appendices B.1.1, B.1.2), and the characterization of additive incentive-compatible pricing mechanisms as linear in character counts (Proposition 5, Theorem 6) is simple, elegant, and yields the pay-per-character prescription.

The empirical work is thorough and well-designed: the plausibility-based heuristic (Algorithm 2) is a convincing proof-of-concept, the utility-gain analysis in Eq. 4 carefully accounts for the GPU cost of verifying plausibility (backed by original energy measurements in Figure 11 / Table 1), and results span multiple model families, temperatures, p values, and languages.

The limitations and broader-impact discussion is unusually honest and substantive, e.g., acknowledging that pay-per-character does not prevent verbosity inflation, that providers could misreport next-token distributions or release a different public tokenizer, and that the heuristic could be misused.
Reproducibility is addressed: hardware, datasets, generation details, licenses, and a code release (footnote 3) are documented, and robustness checks (different prompt samples) are reported.
weaknesses: The central practical premise is questionable: the user receives the output string, and tokenizers for the models studied are public; a user could re-tokenize the returned string to detect token-count misreporting. The paper's threat model assumes users cannot verify tokenizations, and the hardness/plausibility story only bites if users can verify plausibility of next-token probabilities—which the authors themselves concede in Section 5 would require trusted execution or zero-knowledge proofs that do not exist in practice. This significantly weakens the real-world significance of the demonstrated 'vulnerability' and of the proposed remedy.

The headline overcharging numbers are modest and arise only under favorable conditions: temperature > 1.0 (1.15–1.45) and p = 0.99 yield at most ~11% overcharging, with p = 0.95 giving only ~1.8% and p = 0.90 ~0.28% for the best case; common inference settings (lower temperature) are not shown to be exploitable, so the practical impact is narrow.

Experiments use only small open-weight models (1B–8B); the behavior of proprietary models actually deployed under pay-per-token pricing is not evaluated, and the LMSYS Chatbot Arena prompt distribution may not be representative (which the authors acknowledge).

The heuristic algorithm is simple, but no analysis is provided of how far it is from optimal plausible misreporting, and the guarantee is fragile (it falls back to truthful reporting whenever the modified sequence is implausible); alternative attack strategies are not explored.

The incentive-compatibility characterization (Theorem 6) is nearly immediate once string-invariance (Proposition 5) plus additivity are assumed, so the mechanism-design contribution is more of an observation than a deep result; the pay-per-character mechanism also only removes the tokenization incentive, not the verbosity incentive, limiting its practical value as a fix.

The energy-cost model assumes c_gen(t) ≈ c0·len(t) and constant verification cost c_v; while supported empirically, these approximations directly drive the profitability conclusions in Eq. 4, and the marginal-revenue estimates could be sensitive to them.
The code-availability footnote (footnote 3) appears to end without an actual URL in the provided manuscript, which is a reproducibility blemish.
